catalog_quote: ii. The Stress Rule and Its Effects: 1. Alternating Stress Rule - V -> [+stress] / __ { C0 #; (C0 e)^1 C0 V[-stress] } R -> L. Basically, stress placement in St. Francis Abenaki is determined by an alternating stress rule which operates from the end of the word. Stress skips over a non-final schwa and continues alternating from the syllable to the left even if that is also a schwa. However, the personal prefixes ne-, ke-, we- do not carry stress, in which case stress shift will not occur on the syllable to the right. Note the stress patterns in the following: áwasɔ́n 'a piece of firewood', awásɔnál 'firewood (pl.)' ... mekikká 'he barks', nemékilékw 'he barks at me' páskihlá 'he, it bursts open', nepáskenemén 'I burst it' ... sikwán 'spring' ... nepatón 'I bring it', nepásowɔ́ 'I bring him' ... [p. 65] A sequence of two vowels may count as one mora in the stress rule: mskíkkoisál 'lawn…

new_statements.quote: In Western Abenaki the patterns of sentence intonation govern accent, pitch, and segment length. For the work of dictionary making, however, all words spoken in isolation or out of context may be obtained in what is sometimes called the citation intonation. In this pattern the primary accent is on the final syllable and lesser accents fall on every second syllable counting backwards without counting those syllables whose nucleus is e. [examples omitted] The strong accent on the last syllable lengthens the syllable and is accompanied by an extra rise in pitch. [p. xi] ... One speaker consistently moved the usual stress on the final syllable in citation forms back to the penult, but his stress in other intonations conformed to the standard. [p. ix]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (Warne 1975, McGill MA thesis, pp. 64-65) gives an alternating stress rule operating right-to-left from the word end with non-final schwa skipped, all stresses marked alike and no primary designated; its rule field is empty. Day's Pronunciation Guide agrees on the right-edge alternation and the schwa-skipping count, and adds: the FINAL syllable carries the PRIMARY accent in citation forms (with lengthening and a pitch rise), the other accents are 'lesser', the domain is the citation intonation (sentence intonation governs accent otherwise), one speaker had penult citation stress, and an initial schwa syllable can bear secondary accent (matching Warne's 'even if that is al…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In citation (isolation) forms the primary accent falls on the final syllable of the word, which is lengthened and carries an extra pitch rise; lesser (secondary) accents then fall on every second syllable counting leftward from the end, with syllables whose nucleus is the schwa e not counted in the alternation. Outside citation forms, sentence intonation governs accent, pitch and length.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated: 'lesser accents fall on every second syllable counting backwards without counting those syllables whose nucleus is e' (p. xi); a schwa can still be the landing site of a secondary accent: 'In an initial syllable receiving secondary accent e is optionally pronounced like the e in English pet: bedegi come back, menahan island' (p. xii). Final syllables closed by a lax consonant tense and lengthen it 'when they close a strongly accented syllable, which includes all final syllables in the citation intonation' (p. xi).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) The pattern is explicitly the citation-intonation pattern; in connected speech 'the patterns of sentence intonation govern accent, pitch, and segment length' (p. xi). (2) Individual variation: 'One speaker consistently moved the usual stress on the final syllable in citation forms back to the penult, but his stress in other intonations conformed to the standard' (p. ix). (3) Schwa syllables are skipped by the alternating count; unstressed schwa is commonly dropped between consonants, leaving a lengthened preceding consonant (p. ix).
new_statements.identity_note: Day's dictionary is explicitly Western Abenaki as spoken at Odanak (St. Francis, Quebec) and the Missisquoi Bay region in the second half of the 20th century, i.e. west2630, distinguished by Day from Penobscot and the extinct Eastern Abenaki dialects of Maine. The Pronunciation Guide describes the standard citation pattern; one individual speaker with penult citation stress is noted as a deviation (p. ix), and the guide mentions two dialects only with respect to the consonants C and J.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction between sources. Day 1994/1995 (primary accent on the final syllable in citation forms; lesser accents on every second syllable leftward, skipping schwa syllables) is compatible with Warne 1975 in the catalog (alternating R-to-L stress from the word end, non-final schwa skipped, personal prefixes ne-/ke-/we- unstressed) and with LeSourd 2015 already in weak schwas 'skipped over in counting syllables for stress assignment'). The only difference is classificatory: the catalog bundle exits as 'weight-sensitive' because Warne marks all alternating stresses alike, whereas Day designates a fixed final primary and confines the schwa-sensitivity to the secondary accents; Day also adds that outside citation forms sentence intonation governs accent, and records one speaker with penult citation stress.

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim on Warne 1975 pp. 64-65 in the page images we hold. (2) The classification (quantity-sensitive 'weight', full-vs-reduced vowel, right edge, R->L alternating from a stressed final, schwa skipped, person prefixes unstressable) rests on the only formal statement of the rule, and every later linguist statement located (Day 1994 dictionary Pronunciation Guide. LeSourd 2011. LeSourd 2015, downloaded now to independently confirms final primary accent with alternating accents counted leftward skipping schwa-nucleus syllables. Nothing suggests a reclassify. sources.quote: 'Phonologically "weak" occurrences of ə (which are skipped over in counting syllables for stress assignment) are not written by native speakers; they instead write the non-distinctive voicing of obstruents that the presence of these vowels conditions.' Cites Warne 1975 and Day 1994 as the phonological authorities.
